title: TXT and CNAME Records: The Notice Board and the Forwarding Signs
content:
Two DNS record types that most beginners completely ignore — and both of which are consistently among the richest intelligence sources in a professional engagement.

---

**The TXT Record: The Notice Board**

TXT records (Text records) can contain any arbitrary text string. They were originally designed for human-readable notes about a domain. They have since become the standard mechanism for email security configuration and cloud service domain verification — and as a result, they now contain a detailed map of an organisation's cloud vendor relationships.

**The analogy**: TXT records are the notice board attached to the company's public profile. They post notices there for specific technical reasons — email policies, service verifications, security announcements. Anyone walking past can read every notice. The company posted them publicly because the systems that read them need to be able to read them from anywhere.

**What TXT records contain:**

**SPF (Sender Policy Framework)**: A list of servers authorised to send email on behalf of the domain.

Format: 'v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net -all'

What it reveals: Every email sending service the organisation uses. 'include:_spf.google.com' means Google Workspace. 'include:sendgrid.net' means SendGrid for marketing emails. 'include:amazonses.com' means AWS SES. The SPF record is a complete inventory of the organisation's email infrastructure vendors.

**DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance)**: The policy that governs what happens when an email fails authentication.

Format: 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@company.com'

The p= value is the most important field:
— p=none → Monitoring only. Failed emails are delivered. The domain CAN be spoofed in phishing attacks.
— p=quarantine → Failed emails go to spam/junk. Harder to spoof but not impossible.
— p=reject → Failed emails are rejected outright. The strongest protection — domain spoofing will be blocked.

A DMARC policy of p=none is a finding in every professional penetration testing report. It directly enables phishing simulations targeting the organisation's customers or staff.

**Cloud service verification tokens**: When an organisation sets up a cloud service that needs to verify they own a domain, the service asks them to add a specific TXT record. These records are never removed once the service is configured. They accumulate over years.

Common patterns:
— 'MS=ms12345678' → Microsoft 365 domain verification
— 'google-site-verification=abc123' → Google Search Console, Google Workspace
— 'docusign=...' → DocuSign for contracts
— 'SF_domain_auth_...' → Salesforce CRM
— 'atlassian-domain-verification=...' → Jira or Confluence
— 'stripe-verification=...' → Stripe for payments
— 'hubspot-developer-verification=...' → HubSpot CRM

Each verification token is an organisational disclosure: the company uses this vendor. The TXT records tell you the complete stack of cloud services the organisation has ever connected to their domain — including ones they may have discontinued.

---

**The CNAME Record: The Forwarding Signs**

A CNAME record (Canonical Name record) is an alias. Instead of pointing a subdomain directly to an IP address, it points it to another domain name. The DNS system then looks up that other domain name to find the actual IP.

**The analogy**: A CNAME is a forwarding sign inside a building. 'For customer portal services: proceed to Suite 12 at Salesforce Tower on Market Street.' The building doesn't house the service — it redirects you to where the service actually lives.

**What it reveals professionally**:

**CDN relationships**: 'www.company.com CNAME company.cdn.cloudflare.net' means web traffic is proxied through Cloudflare. The actual website runs on different servers. This is the most common CNAME pattern.

**SaaS tool relationships**: Each CNAME is a disclosure of a specific third-party service:
— 'portal.company.com CNAME company.force.com' → Customer portal on Salesforce
— 'blog.company.com CNAME company.wpcomstaging.com' → Blog on WordPress.com
— 'status.company.com CNAME company.statuspage.io' → Status page on Atlassian Statuspage
— 'meet.company.com CNAME ghs.googlehosted.com' → Google Workspace Meet
— 'jobs.company.com CNAME boards.greenhouse.io' → Hiring on Greenhouse

**The dangling CNAME vulnerability**: This is the finding from the case study. When a company cancels a third-party service but does not remove the CNAME record, the destination no longer exists — but the DNS record still directs traffic there. The old destination name is available for anyone to register. If someone claims it, the CNAME now points to their new service — and all traffic to the company's subdomain goes to them.

Finding a dangling CNAME through DNS enumeration:
1. Query the CNAME record for a subdomain
2. The CNAME points to an external domain (e.g. company-old-app.herokuapp.com)
3. Query that external domain — it returns NXDOMAIN (does not exist)
4. Check if the external resource can be claimed
5. If yes: potential subdomain takeover

This vulnerability costs nothing to discover, takes minutes to find through DNS enumeration, and can be used to serve convincing phishing pages from a trusted corporate subdomain.

callouts.title: TXT Record Query Commands
callouts.text:
Query TXT records:
dig TXT meridian-financial.com
nslookup -type=TXT meridian-financial.com (Windows)

Query DMARC specifically (it lives on a subdomain):
dig TXT _dmarc.meridian-financial.com

Query SPF:
dig TXT meridian-financial.com | grep spf

Online tools:
mxtoolbox.com/SuperTool → select TXT Lookup or DMARC Lookup
dmarcian.com/dmarc-inspector → specialised DMARC analysis

callouts.title: Reading the TXT Record Like a Professional
callouts.text:
When you get TXT records back from a query, read them in this order:
1. Find the DMARC record first — p=none is an immediate finding
2. Find the SPF record — list every service in the include: entries
3. List every other TXT record and look up any unfamiliar prefixes

Verification tokens from unknown services are worth researching. 'XY_domain_verification=...' with a quick search often reveals which SaaS product requires that prefix — and therefore which SaaS product the organisation uses.

keyTerms.definition: Text record containing arbitrary string data. Used for email authentication (SPF, DMARC, DKIM) and cloud service domain verification. Accumulates over years as new services are connected. Each verification token is a disclosure of a specific cloud vendor relationship.

An email authentication standard published as a TXT record. Lists which servers are authorised to send email on behalf of the domain. Each 'include:' entry names an email sending service (Google, SendGrid, Amazon SES). A complete inventory of the organisation's email sending infrastructure.

Canonical Name record — an alias that points a domain or subdomain to another domain name instead of directly to an IP address. Reveals CDN providers, SaaS tools, and third-party hosting relationships. A dangling CNAME — one whose destination no longer exists — is a potential subdomain takeover vulnerability.

A CNAME record whose destination domain or cloud resource no longer exists, but the DNS record was never removed. If the destination resource can be claimed (a Heroku app name, S3 bucket, Azure subdomain), the claimant controls what is served from the company's trusted subdomain. Discovered through DNS enumeration and destination validation.
